chapter_theme: In the city of Bhumitilaka the old king has the hearer bow to the lord's feet, then the poem shows the prince Asodharan with women at a lotus pool and his father, the king of kings, who calls him and teaches him not to kill, lie, steal, go to another's wife, or crave wealth got by deceit.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who has heard the sage
the sage whose sermon the king has just heard
the king of kings of the city of Bhumitilaka, father of the prince
the young prince, Sayamathi's son, who plays with the women at the lotus pool
the women given to the prince, who bathe and play with him
the king's attendants who name the prince as the one at the pool
the royal chamberlain who carries orders into the palace

2849.reading: Having heard the sermon of endless dharma, the golden-chested victor tells his people to bow quickly to the lord's feet, for it clears the sins of old births.
2849.nuance: The speaker is not named; the golden-chested victor of line 4 is taken to be Civakan, the hearer of the sermon, and the people addressed are not named.
2849.event: The king, after the sermon, bids his people worship the lord's feet to be rid of the sins of earlier births.

claims.claim: worship of the lord's feet clears the sin gathered through earlier births

2850.reading: The hearer, looking at the sage as at a bright gem held in the palm, sees one who has known what comes and what is past, and says that his flawless sacred words will command them.
2850.nuance: The grammar of the first three lines is hard; who sees and speaks is not named.

2851.reading: A water scene in flowers and pearls: conches graze and let pearls fall, moonlit water breaks the dark, and kazhuneer lilies bloom in the pool as the dhatagi flower is said to grow.
2851.nuance: The words of the last line are obscure; read only as scenery that opens the new place.

2852.reading: Villages ringed by fields are rich: carp leap, swans take fright and fly, and then settle by the open lotus like the white moon joining the sky.

2853.reading: On one side of the mansions the breeze, carrying the smoke of women's hair, passes through areca groves and stands still in the houses like a guest.
2853.nuance: The line about the breeze standing still as 'a halt' is read loosely.

2854.reading: Smoke of aloe and banners crowd the way so that moon and sun cannot find their path, and the city rivals the golden town where the lord of wealth lives.

2855.reading: The city named Bhumitilaka, the ear-ornament of the earth, is a safe and golden place whose streets lie like creepers of desire.

2856.reading: Pavanamadevan, king of kings, joins to women his son Asodharan, whom Sayamathi bore, a lion in learning and like the love-god himself.
2856.nuance: The Tamil says only 'joined to women'; whether this is marriage is not stated. The verse was printed in eight half-lines and joined.
2856.event: King Pavanamadevan gives his son Asodharan women to wed or keep.

2857.reading: Day after day the prince drinks the beauty of the women's mouths and the old wine, and in song and dance and strong drink becomes a victor in the war of love.
2857.event: The prince passes his days in love, music and wine with the women.

2858.reading: When the women's quarrel of love is over, he clasps their small feet while his anklets sing like bees, puts his garland head to them, and takes their charms.
2858.nuance: The end of line 4 turns to a general lament that the unwise let such days pass; the claim is not marked for that reason.
2858.event: The prince wins back the women's favour after a lovers' quarrel.

2859.reading: With the women he goes to the cool lotus lake, and the swans and carp scatter and a flock rises into the sky.
2859.event: The prince and the women reach the lake and frighten off the swans and carp.

2860.reading: A swan flying like a white lotus wreath in the sky, the sky as a woman whose girdle slips as her lover seizes her, and the carp that leap and tear the lotus, make the pool a day-temple.
2860.nuance: The conceit is strained across eight half-lines joined into four; the sense of 'day-temple' is not fixed.

2861.reading: The young swan chicks, like silver cups on a golden dish, press into the golden lotus to hide, but the young lord's eyes find them.
2861.event: Swan chicks hide in the lotus and the prince looks them out.

2862.reading: The chamberlain, bidden to bring those who hide in their right places, gives them to a man and enters the palace, and the youth with the burning spear goes in.
2862.nuance: Who the 'hidden ones' are and who gives and who receives is unclear; read as the swan chicks.
2862.event: The chamberlain gives the hidden ones to one man and the prince enters the palace.

2863.reading: The women, gold as the northern hills, tell the swans that these are not their pools, and hold them to their breasts, stroking and feeding them nectar-milk.
2863.event: The women take the swan chicks to their breasts and tend them.

2864.reading: One day the king of kings sees the party at the lotus pool, asks who has separated them, hears from his attendants that it is the young prince, and orders the spear-bearer brought.
2864.nuance: The Tamil asks who 'separated' them without saying whom; read as the swans and their young.
2864.event: The king sees the prince's party at the pool, asks who has done this, and has the prince summoned.

2865.reading: As drums and lutes sound and the slim-waisted women dance, the attendants tell the seated prince that the lord has sent for him, and he goes and bows at his feet.
2865.event: The prince is told of the summons and goes, hands joined, to his father.

2866.reading: Holding his right shoulder with the left hand and keeping fingers from his mouth, the prince, wearing the ring and bowing his head, bows to the old king.
2866.event: The prince makes the bow of a son before the king.

2867.reading: While women of the bangled hands fan him with whisks, the king, jewelled ear-rings blazing, tells him: if he would hear of the two pains of parting from kin, he must stay and be the seed that grew them.
2867.nuance: The syntax of lines 1-2 is difficult; the speaker and the seed image are read from the last line, where 'the king' ends the sentence, and the sense of 'two kinds of parting' is a best reading.
2867.event: The king begins his lesson to the prince while the women fan him.

2868.reading: The king tells him that when virtue is great and the heart turns to wrong, the dire deeds that swell run and strike, and the killing of life most of all brings great suffering, so he must not kill.
2868.nuance: The verse is the first of five that run on: killing, lying, theft, another's wife, and wealth got by deceit; the same four are named as sins the ascetic guards against at 2824. Here they are taught to a layman prince.

claims.claim: killing a life brings deeds that ripen into great suffering, so it must be shunned

2869.reading: He says that the towers of the upper world rise for the one who speaks true and are lasting, while the towers of the great hell are for the lie; so the prince is bidden to throw lying out.

claims.claim: truthful speech raises one to heaven, falsehood to hell

2870.reading: He says that kings torture a thief, tearing him with the tusks of the lotus-faced elephant, and that the great unseen misery drops him into a fallen birth, so theft and the gambler's trade must be given up.
2870.nuance: The last line pairs theft with gambling (சூது); the reading takes both as to be given up. The lines are hard in parts.

claims.claim: theft is punished by kings here and by a fall to a bad birth hereafter

2871.reading: He says that one who goes to others' wives, who is like a bright sword over his own neck, falls into heavy suffering, and that to put down such unsteady desire is good.

claims.claim: lust for another man's wife brings heavy suffering, so desire must be put down

2872.reading: He says that wealth which, once it is clear, would not take one to the heavenly world is no wealth: gold laughs, the senses laugh, and so does all that earns it.
2872.nuance: The verse was printed in eight half-lines and joined; the lines on laughing gold and senses are read loosely and the argument may be a different one.

claims.claim: wealth that does not lead to heaven or release is not worth the name

2873.reading: He ends by telling the prince to abandon wealth-greed tangled with lies, the dust of deeds, the crooked path, deceit, and the dice cunningly played.

claims.claim: greed for wealth through lies, deceit and gambling must be abandoned

links.note: 2849 has the hearer bid the people bow to the lord's feet to be clear of sins of earlier births; 2846 gave the sermon's release as three together burning the tree of deeds.
links.teaches: The sermon sets release as a burning of deeds, and the hearer answers with worship as the first step, so the doctrine becomes a practice.

links.note: 2861 has the swan chicks hide in the lotus and the prince find them; 2867 has the king speak of the pains of parting from kin.
links.teaches: The play with the chicks is read back as an act of parting kin, so a pleasure-scene becomes a moral one.

links.note: 2824 names lying, killing, theft and lust as what ascetics guard against; 2868 to 2873 teach these to a prince as duties of a layman.
links.teaches: The four sins the ascetic keeps from are given to a layman with their fruits, so the rule is seen to reach a king's son.

links.note: 2868 says killing a life brings great suffering; Kural 321 says not killing is virtuous action and killing brings all other evil.
links.teaches: One tells the rule and the other the fruit, so together the rule has a reason.

gains.a: The verse's warning of suffering gets a plain statement of the rule behind it, that not killing is the chief virtue
gains.b: The Kural's rule gets a scene, a king giving it to a prince who has just scattered the swans, to show who must hear it

links.note: 2868 teaches against killing as a cause of suffering ripening from deeds; Tirumanthiram 200 names killing, theft, lust and lying as sins great as mountains whose giving up reaches Siva's feet.
links.teaches: The same sins are shunned in both, but one pays out as karma and the other as arrival at a god's feet.

gains.a: The Jain king's rule, which has no god to reach, shows the Saiva reward as a different end for the same practice
gains.b: Tirumular's giving-up of the four sins, which says what is gained, shows the Jain view that the fruit is only the working of deeds

links.note: 2869 says the true word lifts to the towers of the upper world and the lie to hell; Kural 293 says that after lying your own heart burns you.
links.teaches: The Kural puts the punishment of a lie within and the verse sets it in the next world, so the two give two places for the same cost.

gains.a: The verse's heaven and hell for speech get an inward witness, the liar's own heart
gains.b: The Kural's burning heart gets a cosmos, in which what the heart knows is carried to a birth

links.note: 2870 says theft is punished by kings and drops the thief into a fallen birth; Kural 290 says the thief loses his footing and the one who does not steal does not lose the world of the gods.
links.teaches: The verse spells the two punishments the Kural gives in one line, in this world and in the next.

gains.a: The verse's king-tortured thief gets the Kural's measure that the loss is of the very footing of life
gains.b: The Kural's lost footing gets a picture, the elephant's tusk and then the fallen birth

links.note: 2870 teaches the giving up of theft and gambling to the prince; Naladiyar 157 says those of faultless vision do not steal, drink, scorn others or lie.
links.teaches: Both put the vows in a list for a lay hearer, so the list of vows seems a common teaching form.

gains.a: The verse's vows get a more general frame, the sort of man who keeps them, 'of faultless vision'
gains.b: The Naladiyar list gets a speaker, a king who gives it to a son with the cost of each breaking

links.note: 2871 says the one who goes to another's wife is like a bright sword over his own neck and falls into heavy suffering; Naladiyar 84 says if caught the leg is cut, the family shamed and hell follows.
links.teaches: Both put the cost of adultery in a worldly punishment and a future one, with the same image of a blade.

gains.a: The verse's blade image gets the actual penalties it stands for, caught, maimed and shamed
gains.b: The Naladiyar's list of penalties gets one picture that holds them, the sword that hangs over him

links.note: 2871 puts another's wife as a sword over the neck and heavy suffering; Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses another's threshold.
links.teaches: The Kural lists four worldly costs and the verse gives one inward one, so the verse adds fear and the Kural adds blame.

gains.a: The verse's suffering gets named costs, enmity and blame, and not only pain
gains.b: The Kural's costs get the Jain view that adultery is also a deed that sends one downward

links.note: 2873 tells the prince to abandon wealth got with lies, deceit and dice; Kural 283 says gain got by stealth seems to grow and then perishes.
links.teaches: The Kural says the ill-gotten gain will not last and the verse adds that the greed behind it is itself what to drop.

gains.a: The verse's abandoning of greed gets a reason from this life, the loss of the gain
gains.b: The Kural's lost gain gets the cause it leaves out, the lie and the dice that win it

source_issues: Verses 2856, 2857, 2858, 2860 and 2872 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verses 2850, 2851, 2853, 2862, 2864 and 2867 to 2872 are hard to parse in places; readings are marked uncertain where the sense turns on it.
The Tamil does not name the speaker of 2849, 2850 or 2867 to 2873; the reading takes the first as Civakan and the later ones as the king.
